title: Geometry - Lesson 7 Practice: Composite Area
description: Practice finding total area by decomposing composite figures into familiar shapes.

questions.question: A composite figure is made of a 7 cm by 5 cm rectangle and a triangle with base 7 cm and height 4 cm. What is the total area?
A large rectangle is 12 m by 8 m. A 3 m by 4 m rectangle is removed. What is the remaining area? Enter just the number.
questions.explanation: Large rectangle: 12 × 8 = 96. Removed part: 3 × 4 = 12. Remaining area: 96 - 12 = 84 m².

questions.question: When decomposition parts overlap, adding all part areas can make the total area too large.
questions.explanation: The overlapping region is counted more than once.

questions.question: A trapezoid has bases 10 cm and 6 cm and height 4 cm. What is its area? Enter just the number.
Which strategy is best for a rectangle with a smaller rectangle cut out from one corner?
options: Large rectangle area minus missing rectangle area
questions.explanation: A cut-out or missing piece should be subtracted from the larger area.

questions.question: A composite figure has a parallelogram with base 9 units and height 5 units plus a rectangle 4 units by 5 units. What is the total area? Enter just the number.
Explain why a triangle with base 8 cm and height 6 cm has area 24 cm² instead of 48 cm².
questions.correctAnswer: A triangle is half of a rectangle or parallelogram with the same base and height, so its area is 1/2 × 8 × 6 = 24 cm².
questions.explanation: A complete answer should mention the one-half factor for triangle area.

questions.question: Describe one reliable way to check that a composite-area decomposition is valid.
questions.correctAnswer: Check that the parts cover the original figure exactly once, with no gaps and no overlaps.
questions.explanation: A valid decomposition should match the original figure exactly.
